title: Periphery wafer on top in leading-edge logic, array beneath
idea: Rearrange the stack: an array-only wafer is hybrid-bonded face-to-face at ~0.5 um pitch to a periphery wafer made in a 3 nm-class GAA logic process, so SAs and sub-wordline drivers are ~5x denser than DRAM-process periphery.
why: Facts 7 and 4: periphery footprint fits under the array, die area -35-45%, array wafer drops ~20 masks. Known in NAND as CBA; new with logic-node periphery.

title: One-time ReRAM-programmed crossbar decoder routes around defects
idea: Substitute hard-wired decoders with a crossbar of HfOx ReRAM switches programmed once at test to connect each address code to any healthy physical row. Decoding and redundancy repair merge into one reconfigurable layer.
why: Yield and periphery: removes separate redundancy decoders and lets any spare row replace any failed row, raising yield on low-cost processes.

title: Overclocker-style margin binning routes weak dies into tolerant tiers
idea: Overclockers prove dies vary widely: an on-die SA margin sweeper characterizes every die at test, and dies that miss JEDEC margins are sold into KV-cache and approximate-memory tiers with relaxed refresh and ECC instead of being scrapped. DUV-only dies with wider variation stay economical.
why: Usable supply +5-10% from the same wafers, offsetting the variability penalty of non-EUV processes.

title: Plumber's backflow: hand restored bitline charge to the next mat
idea: A plumber never dumps hot water that could preheat the next tank. When one mat closes, its bitlines still at VDD are briefly shorted to the rising bitlines of the next mat being sensed, handing over about half their charge before the supply finishes the restore.
why: Cuts bitline restore energy ~20-30% per activate, a large part of the ~5.9 pJ per useful bit random read (fact 8).

title: Spin-orbit voltage readout: nanomagnets drive inverters, no sense amps
idea: Constraint: non-volatile magnetic bits. Instead of current-mode TMR sensing, pass a small supply current through the bit's spin-injection layer into a strong spin-orbit layer (Bi2Se3/Pt), where the inverse Edelstein/spin-Hall effect converts spin to a charge voltage whose sign follows magnetization (MESO-style); that voltage gates a local inverter directly, with no reference or SA.
why: Periphery (fact 7): deletes SAs and references. Risk: ~10-100 mV output and spin-to-charge efficiency.

title: WaterSense label for chips: grants priced per liter per gigabyte
idea: EPA's WaterSense label made low-flow fixtures mainstream. Define an audited liters-per-GB metric and tie CHIPS-style grants, tax credits and federal procurement preference to tiers (top tier <=10% of the 2025 baseline), which rewards dry periphery flows, weak-signal sensing that simplifies capacitors, and wafer reuse.
why: Water/U.S. manufacturability: the 10x target becomes a funded design rule, pulling dry tools and periphery redesigns into U.S. fabs where water permits limit siting.

title: Deliberately weakened canary cells trigger refresh on physical decay
idea: Substitute timer-driven refresh with physical sensing: each mat carries replica canary cells with ~30% smaller Cs and a longer-leakage access device, read by a dedicated sense amp. A mat refreshes only when its canary flips, so the interval follows the real temperature and leakage.
why: Refresh (fact 3): at typical datacenter temperatures retention is far above the 32/64 ms worst case, so refresh energy and bandwidth loss drop 50-80%.

title: Ferroelectric trim transistor nulls each sense amp's offset
idea: Inverting 'sense-amp offset is frozen at fabrication': one HZO ferroelectric trim FET in each sense amp's tail is programmed once at wafer test to cancel its measured offset, so the latch can use minimum-size transistors and resolve ~40 mV instead of ~100 mV.
why: Sense-amp area -30-40%, or alternatively ~2x less required cell charge, easing the 60-75:1 capacitor aspect-ratio wall.

title: Spend periphery to buy back the capacitor: 16-cell bitlines
idea: Reverse the classic trade of long bitlines to save sense amps: use 16-cell bitlines (Cbl ~0.4 fF) with SAs placed under the array, so a planar or shallow ~1 fF capacitor gives the same transfer ratio a 5 fF pillar gives today.
why: Fact 1: eliminates the 60-75:1 pillar etch and exotic high-k; capacitor module steps -30-40%. Requires SA-under-array at ~4x today's SA density.

title: Periodic action: lock-in readout of varactor cells, no destructive read
idea: TRIZ #19 Periodic action: each storage element is a floating MOS varactor whose small-signal capacitance depends on its stored charge (accumulation versus depletion); a ~10 MHz small excitation on the wordline and a lock-in demodulator shared by 256 bitlines read that capacitance without moving the stored charge, so reads are non-destructive.
why: 100x path: deletes restore/write-back circuits and per-bitline sense amps (256:1 sharing) and allows planar cells stacked in 8+ BEOL tiers on mature or display-class lines; trade-offs: ~1 us reads and lower density per tier. Also removes Fact 8's destructive read.

title: Microwave dispersive readout senses cells without draining them
idea: Ideal result: a read that costs nothing and leaves the bit untouched. Borrowing qubit readout, make each bitline segment part of a GHz resonator; a storage node gating a tiny varactor shifts the resonance, and a picowatt probe tone reflected from the line reveals the bit with no charge sharing and no restore.
why: Destructive read and CV^2 energy (facts 8, 10): no restore cycle and no full-swing bitline; target <0.5 pJ per useful bit versus ~5.9 pJ.

title: Completion-detecting sense amps make access time average, not worst case
idea: Ideal result: a read that takes exactly as long as that bit needs. Each SA stripe adds a done-detector on replica latches that signals when regeneration completes; the controller uses an asynchronous handshake instead of a fixed worst-case tRCD.
why: Latency and bandwidth: typical cells have ~2x margin over the worst case, so average tRCD falls ~30%.

title: Monk's quiet hour: sense strobes dodge output-driver noise
idea: A monk prays when the monastery is quiet. An on-die scheduler knows when other banks' read bursts switch the DQ drivers and shifts each sense-amp strobe by up to ~500 ps inside tRCD slack so latching never coincides with output supply noise.
why: Removes the I/O-noise term (~10-15 mV) from the sense budget, spendable as smaller Cs or longer bitlines (facts 1, 7).

title: Electrohydrodynamic-jet printed nano-copper microbumps for memory stacking
idea: Worse: run lithography, seed, plating and etch steps to form every microbump. Flip: EHD-jet-print copper nanoparticle pillars at ~10 um pitch directly onto pads and sinter them in a maskless additive bumping step.
why: HBM cost and capital (fact 6): removes bump masks and plating lines, with denser I/O at lower capex.

title: Recompute-on-decay replaces refresh for training activation stashes
idea: Jump from the cell timescale to the training-job timescale: activations stashed for the backward pass get no refresh; each 64 B block carries parity plus a weak-sense flag, and any flagged block is regenerated by re-running its forward segment from the nearest checkpoint, as gradient checkpointing already does.
why: Activation stashes are ~30-60% of training memory; zero refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3) for <1% recompute, since most stashes live <1 s.

title: Block-copolymer self-assembled gates for near-zero-LER sense-amp transistors
idea: Define only the sense-amp input-pair gates with directed self-assembly of a lamellar block copolymer guided by a coarse litho trench; the molecularly set period gives ~1 nm line-edge roughness instead of ~2-3 nm from resist. Both transistors of a pair are cut from the same lamella so they share edge statistics.
why: SA offset sets the minimum bitline signal; halving LER-driven mismatch cuts required signal ~30%, allowing ~1.4x longer bitlines (fewer SA strips, ~8-10% die) or a smaller capacitor.

title: Eliminate the decoder tree: colliding-pulse time-of-flight row selection
idea: Launch pulses from both ends of a slow-wave RC delay line that runs past 512 wordline taps. The relative launch delay encodes the address and sets where the two pulses meet, and only at that tap does the summed amplitude exceed a threshold inverter that fires its wordline.
why: Replaces predecoders and decoders (~4-6% of die, ~13 address wires per mat) with 2 wires and one threshold device per row. Needs ~10 ps/row timing accuracy with PVT calibration.

title: Bit-significance placement with per-subarray voltage and refresh
idea: Give each subarray its own VARY tap and refresh rate set by mode register; the memory controller places AI tensors' sign and exponent bits in strong, often-refreshed subarrays and low-order mantissa bits in low-voltage, rarely refreshed ones.
why: Refresh and voltage (facts 3, 10): ~40% lower array energy for weights and KV caches with negligible accuracy loss.

title: Segmentation: above-array oxide switches slice each bitline into eight
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation resolves 'long bitline for few sense amps' versus 'short bitline for big signal': row-address-controlled IGZO isolation switches, built in BEOL above the array at zero silicon area, cut each bitline every 64 cells so only the segment holding the active row is connected to the sense amp.
why: Facts 1 and 7: effective bitline capacitance drops ~8x and the transfer ratio rises ~5x, so either sense-amp count falls ~4-8x (periphery ~49% to ~30% of die) or capacitor aspect ratio can relax from ~70:1 to ~20:1.

title: Token-passing row sequencer replaces the random-access row decoder
idea: Reverse random access into order: for AI-weight and KV-cache streaming parts, rows open as a token shifts one wordline per step through a shift-register chain with a small jump table, deleting the NAND-tree row decoder and its pitch-limited predecode buses.
why: Fact 7: row decoders ~8-10% of die -> ~1-2%; activations pipeline back-to-back and decode power drops ~90%; random access survives at bank granularity.

title: Xerographic dry printing of periphery power and global routing
idea: Xerography means 'dry writing': image the periphery's relaxed-pitch (>=300 nm) global/power metal pattern onto a charged photoconductive transfer drum, pick up copper-nanoparticle 'toner' electrostatically, transfer it to the wafer and laser-sinter in forming gas. No resist, plating bath, CMP or post-CMP clean.
why: Water: the top 3-4 periphery metal layers (damascene plating, CMP and scrub rinses) need ~10x less UPW, and plating/CMP chemical waste disappears. Resolution and adhesion are the risks.

title: Biased-reference sentinel column detects disturbance before data cells flip
idea: Effect: deliberately offset sense threshold as a disturbance canary. In a small team's memory macro, each row has one sentinel cell whose sense amp uses a shifted reference (~30% of nominal signal), rewritten to 1 at every refresh; it fails before any data cell under leakage or hammer disturbance, so a flipped sentinel triggers immediate refresh of that row and its neighbors.
why: Row hammer and refresh (facts 3, 9): one cell per row (~0.1% area) replaces counter tables and acts as a built-in canary for longer default refresh.

title: Rank-modulation sensing via winner-take-all on charge order
idea: Store data as the ORDER of charge levels among a group of cells, read by a winner-take-all network that finds which cells hold the most charge. Uniform leakage at 125 C lowers all charges together but preserves order, so no absolute reference is needed.
why: Retention at hot (fact 3) decouples from absolute charge; refresh interval can stretch several-fold, and MLC-like density becomes possible.

title: Hydraulics: electrolyte-gated printed sense transistors on roll-to-roll film
idea: TRIZ #29 Pneumatics and hydraulics: the solid gate dielectric of the sense and decode circuits is replaced by a printed ion-gel electrolyte whose double-layer capacitance (~10 uF/cm2) gives high transconductance below 1 V, so inkjet- or gravure-printed oxide transistors at 5-10 um can still amplify millivolt bitline signals.
why: 100x path: periphery is printed on film at ~$1-10/m2 with no vacuum fab, pairing with nanoimprinted array films; trade-offs: ionic response of ~1-10 us, temperature sensitivity and large area. Attacks capital intensity (Fact 4) and U.S. manufacturability.

title: Nanocryotron sense amps for 4-kelvin DRAM
idea: Revive Buck's 1956 cryotron in its modern form, the superconducting nanowire nTron. At 4 K a DRAM cell retains data for hours, and an NbN nanowire biased near its critical current switches to the normal state when the bitline's charge-sharing current adds to it, giving >1,000x gain at zero static power. Decoders become nTron trees, which removes CMOS periphery heat from the cold stage.
why: Removes refresh (fact 3) and slashes sense energy for quantum and superconducting computers, which lack dense cold memory today. Niche, but no incumbent holds it.

title: Dynamic row-well back-biasing replaces the 3 V wordline pump
idea: Inverting 'the access transistor needs a 3 V wordline': each row's access transistors sit in an isolated well that is driven with the wordline, strongly reverse-biased when off and forward-biased when selected, so a 1.2 V wordline swing gives the same on-current and off-leakage.
why: Removes VPP charge pumps (~5-8% of periphery area and notable power) and cuts wordline CV^2 ~6x; attacks the voltage floor.

title: Nanoimprint templates pattern decoder and sub-wordline-driver stripes
idea: Patterned-media hard drives and RFID makers imprint sub-20 nm features cheaply; the highly regular decoder and SWD stripes are imprinted from a master template at 15-20 nm half-pitch, while irregular logic stays on DUV at relaxed rules.
why: Pitch-critical periphery layers made without EUV at ~1/4 the tool cost (fact 4 capital intensity).

title: Electric-fish lock-in sensing via carrier-modulated cell plate and chopper demodulation
idea: Weakly electric fish detect nanovolt fields by emitting a carrier and demodulating synchronously. During the read window the bitline precharge reference carries a small GHz carrier, and a chopper switch pair at the sense-amp input demodulates it, moving the signal away from 1/f noise and slow offset drift before the latch fires.
why: Fact 1/10: removing offset and low-frequency noise (~30-40 mV equivalent) gives ~1.5-2x effective SNR. That buys ~40% smaller Cs, or VARY below 1 V for lower CV^2 energy.

title: Blessing in disguise: Geiger-mode avalanche bitline sensing of 100-electron cells
idea: TRIZ #22 Blessing in disguise turns breakdown, normally a failure, into gain: each bitline segment ends in a SPAD-like junction biased just above avalanche breakdown, which a stored packet of ~100 electrons triggers into a full-swing self-quenched pulse, so storage nodes need only ~0.02 fF and can be plain planar diffusions.
why: 100x path: deletes the capacitor module (Fact 1) and allows near-4F2 planar or stacked cells on mature nodes; trade-offs: dark counts and afterpulsing need repeat reads and strong ECC, ~10-100 ns quench recovery and higher sense voltage. Attacks Facts 1, 2 and 4.

title: Geiger-mode avalanche sense node gives digital output from 100 electrons
idea: Bias a tiny junction just above breakdown with a quench resistor; a '1' cell injects hundreds of carriers that trigger avalanche with near-unity probability, a '0' injects none, so the sense node outputs a full-rail digital pulse with no linear amplifier. Dark-count false triggers are handled by a short gated window plus ECC.
why: Cs could fall ~100x (fact 1) and the SA collapses to a quench + latch; strong density and periphery-area gain if dark counts can be tamed.

title: Po: a photon-counter sense amp — Geiger-mode silicon junction
idea: Po: a sense amp as sensitive as a photon counter. Gate a pair of small Si p+/n junctions just above breakdown (Geiger mode, as in a SPAD) during sensing; the bitline differential biases which side avalanches first, the avalanche current latches that side, and a doped-poly quench resistor resets it.
why: Periphery (#7) and capacitor wall (#1): ~1e5 intrinsic junction gain from two devices, so tiny signals suffice; Si, B, P only. Dark counts and afterpulsing are the risk.

title: Fleet-learned per-bank sense timing pushed by firmware
idea: Scale jump to the datacenter and to years: every module reports per-bank minimum passing tRCD/tRAS from periodic margin sweeps, the fleet models them by vendor lot, temperature and age, and firmware pushes per-bank timing tables back, re-tightening or relaxing as drift appears.
why: Typical banks carry 30-50% timing slack, so ~20-30% lower latency and activation energy fleet-wide with no new silicon (facts 7, 10).

title: Latch resolution time as free soft information for decoding
idea: Time-domain readout: because a latch resolves in ~tau*ln(V/dV), a strobe flip-flop samples each SA output a few hundred ps before the normal strobe, flags any SA not yet resolved as weak, and feeds the flags as erasures to the decoder on the base die.
why: Erasures cost half an error, so the decoder tolerates ~2x more marginal reads, letting SAs shrink or bitlines lengthen (facts 1, 7); ~10-20% sense-area cut or ~1.5x lower Cs.

title: Ice-cream sandwich: U.S. mature-node periphery wafers bonded to arrays
idea: Split every die into an array-only wafer (cells, bitlines, capacitors) and a periphery wafer (SAs, decoders, pumps, I/O) built on existing U.S. 28-40 nm logic lines, joined by wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding with one bond per bitline staggered along its length (a ~50 um bitline has ~1.5 um2 of footprint, room for a 1 um-pitch pad).
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: the ~49% periphery needs no EUV and moves to depreciated U.S. fabs, freeing ~40% of scarce DRAM-fab wafer area per bit and letting new array-only fabs skip most logic steps (~30% less capex).

title: NEMS relay latch inside the sub-wordline driver
idea: Replace the sub-wordline driver's level shifter and pull-down with a nanoelectromechanical relay whose mechanical hysteresis both latches the wordline state and gives true zero off-leakage; low-voltage decode pulls it in and it switches the 3 V VPP line directly.
why: Voltage floor and periphery leakage (facts 10, 7): removes level-shifter area and the SWD leakage that dominates standby, and gives a perfectly held negative wordline on idle rows.

title: Eliminate deep-trench decoupling capacitors with traveling-wave sense-amp firing
idea: Fire the 8k SAs of a row as a wave crossing the mat over ~2 ns, each SA enabling its neighbor through a delay cell, so the 1-2 A sensing spike becomes a flat ramp. Supply droop falls ~5x, so deep-trench decaps (which need SF6 Bosch etch) and most MOS decaps are deleted; the remaining flow uses Cl-based etches.
why: Removes ~2-4% of die in decaps, and the lower droop lets the array voltage margin shrink (fact 10); the first-needed column is fired first to hide latency.

title: Venetian blinds: bit-plane layout fetches only requested precision bits
idea: Tilt Venetian blinds to let in only the light you want. Store tensors transposed into bit-planes across column groups, with a precision-select field in the column command so a 4-bit or 8-bit inference read opens only those planes' micro-rows and moves only those bits, not the full 16-bit words.
why: Activation plus transfer energy scales with bits actually needed: 2-4x from precision alone, and >10x when combined with micro-row activation that already removes overfetch.

title: Sn: tin-oxide Schottky diode matrices revive core-memory predecoding
idea: Spray-pyrolyze SnO2 films in air over the decoder region and form Schottky diode AND matrices, the 1950s diode-ROM decoding style, so row predecoding is done by stacked two-terminal devices and only final drivers stay in silicon.
why: Moves predecoder transistor area up and off the die plane (~5% die area, fact 7) with an air process and no critical lithography or rare gases.

title: Zero-entropy token row selection for AI weight streaming memory
idea: AI inference reads weights in a fixed order, so the address entropy per access is ~0 bits; a full row decoder supplies log2(N) bits of random choice that are wasted. Replace decoders with a pitch-matched shift-register token that walks rows sequentially, keeping only coarse random access at mat level.
why: Periphery (fact 7) and energy: row decode area ~70-90% smaller in a streaming tier, plus predictable access removes most precharge/activate overhead.

title: Po: wordlines latch themselves — vertical Si thyristor drivers
idea: Po: a wordline driver that needs only a nudge. Replace each sub-wordline driver's high-voltage CMOS pair with a vertical p-n-p-n silicon thyristor at wordline pitch: a small decoder pulse triggers it, it regenerates and holds the wordline high through a shared weak bleed, and a common reset pulse turns all off.
why: Periphery (#7): sub-wordline driver strips (~10% of die) shrink ~3x because vertical thyristors need no thick-oxide PMOS or well spacing; Si, B, P only.

title: Roll-to-roll laminated microchannel film cools hot periphery strips
idea: Worse: let pumps, PHYs and base-die logic heat the array so refresh doubles above 85 C. Flip: laminate a roll-to-roll-embossed polymer microchannel film with printed manifolds onto the stack, routing coolant directly over hot periphery strips and keeping array tiers below ~70 C.
why: Refresh (fact 3): staying out of the 2x-refresh temperature range halves refresh energy and bandwidth loss in HBM.

title: Bucket-brigade CCD columns feed one floating diffusion per column
idea: For a streaming tier, arrange each 512-cell column as a charge-coupled shift register that clocks charge packets to a single floating-diffusion readout at the column end, as 1970s CCD memories did, but with modern 0.5 fF sense nodes reading ~1k e- packets.
why: Periphery collapses to one sense node per column, no per-bitline SA (fact 7); very high density for sequential workloads.

title: Electrostatic NEMS relays build zero-leakage row decoders above the array
idea: Effect: electrostatic pull-in hysteresis. Build BEOL TiN or poly-SiGe nano-relays (pull-in ~1-2 V) arranged as a relay-tree row decoder; hysteresis holds the selected path with no static current, and the metal contacts pass the 3 V wordline level directly, so no level shifters are needed.
why: Periphery area/leakage (fact 7): decoder and level-shifter area moves to BEOL and off-state leakage is zero in standby.

title: Phase-change repair registers replace laser-fuse banks and their latches
idea: Effect: thermal hysteresis of the amorphous/crystalline phase change. Store redundancy repair addresses in small GST or Sb2Te3-superlattice cells in BEOL, programmed once at test by an on-die micro-heater pulse and read directly by the decoder compare logic. This eliminates pitch-limited laser-fuse banks and the boot-time fuse broadcast latches.
why: Periphery area (fact 7) and capital: ~2-3% of die area recovered and the laser-repair tool step removed.

title: Plywood veneer: Smart-Cut array laminates share one periphery base
idea: Like plywood glued from thin veneers, transfer thin 180 nm array layers (cells and bitline selects only, no periphery) one at a time onto a periphery base wafer using 1995 Smart-Cut hydrogen splitting and oxide bonding. Each veneer's bitlines drop through vertical vias to the shared SA/decoder base.
why: Periphery is built once for 8-16 layers, so array efficiency nears 90% and density scales with layer count instead of lithography: a U.S. 200 mm-fab path to dense memory.

title: Sense amp with nonvolatile ferroelectric offset trim
idea: Integrate a tiny HZO ferroelectric capacitor in each sense amp and program its polarization at wafer test so it couples a compensating charge onto the weak side of the latch, permanently trimming offset from ~15 mV to ~3 mV with no runtime calibration.
why: Sense margin (facts 1, 7): lower offset allows ~40% smaller SA devices, or ~2x longer bitlines (half the SA stripes), or smaller Cs.

title: Eliminate PFAS permitting drag: fluorine-free periphery fast-lane policy
idea: Create a federal/state permitting fast lane and cost share for DRAM periphery lines certified fluorine-free (Cl/Br/O etches, MoO2Cl2 metal, PAG-free resists, Cl2/O2 chamber cleans, PFPE-free test). Publish it as an open reference flow with shared yield data, so new U.S. periphery fabs avoid PFAS-driven permit delays and EU restriction risk.
why: Permitting is ~1-2 years of a 3-5-year fab timeline. Paired with array-only fabs, this puts ~49% of DRAM die area into plants that are faster to build in the U.S.

title: Mg: water-dissolved magnesium sacrificial spacer creates air-gap bitlines
idea: Evaporate a thin Mg sacrificial spacer between bitlines, cap it with a porous lid, and dissolve it in dilute carbonated water to leave air gaps, avoiding the XeF2 (xenon) or argon-plasma release normally used for air gaps.
why: Bitline coupling falls ~40%, raising the transfer ratio Cs/(Cs+CB) (fact 1) so twice as many cells share an SA (fact 7) or Cs can drop.

title: Eliminate the on-die command decoder: host drives raw array timing
idea: Remove the DRAM's command state machine, mode registers and timing counters. The die exposes raw controls (wordline enable, SA enable, precharge, column strobe) on a hybrid-bonded wide port. The host controller issues every edge with row-specific timing from a per-row strength map built by boot-time profiling.
why: Removes ~2-3% of area in command logic and cuts per-row tRCD/tRAS ~20-35%, since most rows are far from worst case. A new array generation also needs no new on-die logic.

title: Eliminate address buses: two-wire analog voltage row addressing
idea: Replace the ~13 predecoded address lines per mat with two analog wires (16 coarse and 32 fine levels) and a resistive ladder. Each wordline driver ANDs two 2-transistor window comparators tied to its ladder taps and fires only when both broadcast voltages fall in its window; the wiring is Cl-etched Mo.
why: Removes the predecoders (decoder area -40%) and the metal level that hosts the address bus; noise margin needs ladder calibration.

title: One-hot token ring steps refresh without waking address decoders
idea: Worse: run the full row decoder and predecode buses for every refresh command. Flip: a one-hot shift chain embedded in the wordline driver strip passes a token row to row during refresh and streaming scans, so decoders and global address buses stay power-gated.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3): periphery share of refresh energy cut ~25-35%.

title: Micro-LED light selects mats through the silicon backside
idea: Scale jump from datacenter optics to on-die addressing: a micro-LED array on the package lid shines 1.3 um light through thinned silicon onto Ge photodiodes at each mat's driver enable, so mat selection arrives as light and the global decoders and address buses disappear.
why: Eliminates global address wiring and part of the decoder periphery (~3-5% area, fact 7) and its switching energy; helps 3D stacks where vertical wiring is scarce.

title: Pop-up-book sense amplifier: vertical-channel latch fits bitline pitch
idea: Like a pop-up book that stands flat art upright, build the SA cross-coupled pair and equalizer from vertical-channel transistors in a two-tier stack (n-latch below, p-latch above). One complete SA then fits under a single 2F bitline pitch instead of a 4-6F-wide strip.
why: Shrinks SA-strip footprint ~3-4x (SA strips are ~10-15% of die) and enables open-bitline 4F^2 arrays without an SA-pitch crisis.

title: Options trading: speculative early latch with cancellable confirmation
idea: Like buying an option, a small fast SA latches at ~40% signal development and ships data early; the main SA finishes at full development and, on the rare disagreement, sends a cancel/replay token on the data bus, like exercising the option.
why: Latency: ~30% faster tRCD on most reads, with replays rare (<1e-4) when references are centred.

title: N: certified rare-gas-free periphery lines under CHIPS funding
idea: Create a federal certification and cost-share for N2/H2-only periphery lines: solid-state-laser or LED lithography, N2-purged ALD, H2-carrier CVD, electroplating, and H2 or N2 backside wafer cooling instead of helium; DRAM makers buying bonded periphery from such lines earn credits.
why: Insulates U.S. memory output from Qatar helium and neon supply shocks and seeds U.S. periphery capacity (U.S. manufacturability).

title: Si: silicon delay-line sensing tolerates variable rare-gas-free transistors
idea: Convert bitline voltage into delay by letting it bias the footer of a 16-stage current-starved Si inverter chain, then race it against a reference chain in a time-to-digital arbiter; averaging across 16 stages tolerates the larger device variation of periphery patterned with gas-free LED or solid-state-laser lithography.
why: Allows ~0.6 V sensing (fact 10) and relaxed periphery patterning; claims ~2x lower offset sensitivity than a single latch.

title: Stacked thin-oxide cascode wordline drivers survive 125 C TDDB
idea: TDDB life shrinks exponentially with field and temperature, so 3 V drivers need thick, slow, large oxides. Split the swing across two series thin-oxide devices with a mid-rail cascode bias so each oxide sees ~1.5 V, inside its 10 y TDDB limit at 125 C.
why: Driver area ~2x smaller and faster than thick-oxide drivers (fact 7), with no lifetime penalty at hot.

title: MRI gradient row selection with window-conducting access devices
idea: MRI picks one slice with a field gradient, not one wire per slice. Use anti-ambipolar access devices (e.g. MoS2/WSe2 heterojunctions) that conduct only inside a narrow gate window; a resistive ladder spreads a voltage gradient across a mat's wordlines, and two DAC-set endpoint voltages place exactly one row in that window.
why: Replaces row decoders and most sub-wordline drivers (~15-20% of die) with two DACs per mat (fact 7).

title: Charge-trap-trimmed sense amps: offset fixed once, transistors minimum size
idea: Failure mined: MRAM ventures such as Spin Memory could not shrink their arrays because low-TMR signals needed huge low-offset sense amps (offset scales as 1/sqrt(area)). Fix: put a nitride charge trap in each sense-amp input transistor's gate stack and program it at wafer test, with field recalibration, to null the offset. SA devices can then be minimum size, and the same trick works for DRAM sense amps.
why: Halves to quarters SA area, or lets the cell signal fall ~3x for a smaller capacitor (fact 1): ~5% of die area or a shallower capacitor.

title: Electron-beam-addressed charge film (EBAM) with field-emitter arrays
idea: Failure mined: 1970s EBAM/BEAMOS (GE, Control Data) stored bits as charge written and read by an electron beam on a MOS target, and died on vacuum, beam deflection and slow serial access. Fix: replace the deflected beam with a CMOS-driven Spindt field-emitter array in which each tip covers a 64x64 patch at 8 nm spot pitch through a small electrostatic microlens. Bits are charge in a nitride film, read by beam-induced current to a common backplate.
why: 10x at the same cost: no per-bit access transistor, wordline or bitline. An 8 nm bit pitch on an unpatterned film is ~13x DRAM density, and the only patterning is the emitter array at a relaxed ~200 nm pitch (no EUV).

title: Eliminate vias in decoder routing: capacitively coupled dynamic signal layers
idea: Decoder and predecoder signals are pulses, so let them cross metal levels through overlap capacitors with 5 nm ALD Al2O3 between the layers instead of vias, with a keeper on each node restoring DC level. Only power rails use vias, placed in a few relaxed landing zones etched with BCl3/Cl2, and the wiring is subtractive Cl-etched Mo.
why: Removes most periphery via etches (normally fluorocarbon), barrier and fill steps; periphery BEOL cost ~-20% and via-yield failures disappear.

title: Legacy DDR4 dies aggregated by a 28nm CXL base
idea: Co-package 8-16 dies from mature DDR4 lines on a 28 nm logic base that runs the DDR4 cores slowly but wide in parallel and exposes a CXL memory interface, taking over refresh management, ECC and hammer mitigation in the base.
why: Supply and capital (fact 4): turns trailing DDR4 capacity into a usable server memory tier at near-zero capex; base dies can be made in U.S. trailing fabs.

title: Decoding moves to the controller; DRAM receives one-hot row lines
idea: Reverse where address decoding happens: a logic base die performs row predecode and sends one-hot group-select lines through dense hybrid-bond pads to each array tile; the DRAM die keeps only the final AND gates at the wordline drivers.
why: Fact 7: row/column decoder and address-latch area (~6-8%) leaves the DRAM die; logic-node decode is faster and lower power.

title: Multi-threshold soft-sensing sense amps feed LDPC decoder in base die
idea: Box: shrunk 2.5 fF cap x Si access x 3-reference soft sensing x HBM base-die decoder x bulk Si x standard. Each SA compares against three references and ships a 2-bit log-likelihood value; a rate-0.89 LDPC decoder in the logic base die corrects a 1% raw cell BER to <1e-15 (BSC capacity at p=0.01 is ~0.92).
why: Tolerating 1% lets Cs halve (AR ~60:1 to ~30:1) and SA offset relax, for ~11% parity overhead.

title: Base-camp pumps: HBM core dies take rails from base die
idea: Mountaineers leave heavy gear at base camp. Move VPP, VBB and VBLP charge pumps and regulators from every HBM core die into the logic base die, built as efficient switched-capacitor converters on better transistors, and deliver the rails up dedicated power TSVs.
why: Frees ~4-8% of each core die and roughly doubles pump efficiency (facts 6, 7, 10); the HBM PHY is untouched.

title: Librarian's central catalog: base-die NVM holds all repair maps
idea: A librarian keeps one catalog, not a card box on every shelf. Redundancy and trim data for every HBM core die live in nonvolatile memory on the logic base die (embedded RRAM or MTP) and are broadcast up the TSVs at power-up, deleting the fuse banks from each core die.
why: Fuse and antifuse banks cost ~2-4% of core die area; removing them adds density and lets repair be updated after stacking (facts 6, 7).

title: Bucket-brigade row shifting replaces column decoders
idea: Inverting 'columns are picked by a decoder and mux': after sensing, the row buffer is shifted toward the I/O edge through a latch chain like a CCD image sensor, so data streams out in order without column-select lines or decoders; random columns use 16-position skip taps.
why: Removes column decoders and CSL wiring (~8-12% of periphery) and suits streaming AI tensor reads, at some random-access latency cost.

title: Acoustic delay-line page buffer frees sense amps instantly
idea: A modern mercury delay line: an AlN surface-acoustic-wave track runs under each bank's I/O edge. A sensed row is launched as acoustic pulses that take ~100 ns to cross, during which the sense amps precharge and open the next row; a transducer at the far end recaptures the bits as they arrive and serves bursts in flight.
why: Hides precharge and row-cycle time and replaces SRAM row caches in the periphery, for ~1.5x effective bank bandwidth on streaming loads.

title: Bitlines as last-gasp battery for finishing in-flight NV writes
idea: Constraint: no write may be torn when power dies. At power-fail detect, switches tie every precharged bitline and VPP-node capacitance on the die (~3 uF total at 0.5-3 V) to a shared rail that powers completion of in-flight NV writes and a write-buffer flush.
why: Gives ~0.5-1 uJ, enough for ~0.5 MB of MRAM writes, from capacitance already on the die, removing NVDIMM supercaps and external hold-up.

title: In-sense-amp capacitor taps shield finite-endurance NV cells from writes
idea: Constraint: NV cells (FeRAM/MRAM, ~1e10-1e12 cycles) must still behave with DRAM-class endurance. Each sense amp gets four capacitor taps that act as an in-SA DRAM row cache; writes coalesce there, and a row is written to the NV array only on eviction or at power-fail, flushed with an on-die energy reserve.
why: Turns 1e10-cycle NV cells into effectively unlimited-endurance memory for hot rows, at <5% SA-stripe overhead.

title: Universal programmable sense front-end die for any capacitorless array
idea: Inverting 'periphery is designed for one cell type': a merchant logic die with sense channels configurable in current, voltage, or time mode is hybrid-bonded to any capacitorless array (thyristor, FeFET, floating-body, MTJ), so new cell startups only build arrays.
why: Removes ~2-3 years and most periphery design cost from each new memory technology and gives a volume product for US logic fabs.

title: Leaky charge-packet activation counter cell in every row
idea: Inverting 'row-hammer tracking needs digital counters': each row gets one extra cell in a counter column that receives a fixed charge packet on every activation instead of being restored; the same sense amp compares it to a threshold during activate, refreshing neighbors and resetting it when crossed, while natural leakage forgets old activations like a sliding window.
why: Replaces multi-bit per-row counters and read-modify-write (as in activation-counting schemes) with one cell per row, closing ~1k-activation hammer exposure at <0.1% area.

title: Coincident half-pulse wordline select borrowed from Apollo core memory
idea: Core memories selected a bit where two half-currents met; two half-amplitude pulses launched from opposite ends of a bank-wide transmission line meet at a sub-array chosen by their relative delay, and only there does the sum exceed the local access threshold. Local decoders vanish.
why: Local row decoders removed (fact 7) with no fine litho; speculative because it needs ~10 ps timing precision.

title: Self-assembled stochastic nanowire decoders calibrated at wafer test
idea: Molecule-to-wafer jump: block-copolymer self-assembly patterns sub-10 nm address nanowires with random doping codes instead of lithographed decoders, and at wafer test each chip learns once which code reaches which row and stores it in a small address-translation table.
why: Decoder layers without EUV (fact 4) and decoders dense enough for 4F2/3D pitch (fact 7); costs ~20% of the code space.

title: Camel-nose countercurrent cascade rinses for periphery wet benches
idea: A camel's nasal turbinates recover exhaled water by countercurrent exchange. Plumb periphery wet benches as 4-stage countercurrent cascades: fresh UPW enters only the final rinse and its overflow feeds the stage before, with inline resistivity/TOC sensors advancing wafers instead of timed overflow; periphery's relaxed contamination spec permits it.
why: Water: rinse water per periphery clean falls ~8-12x (efficiency compounds with stage count) with no new chemistry.

title: Po: a sense amp with moving parts — bistable Si nanobeam
idea: Po: a sense amplifier with moving parts. A buckled, bistable single-crystal Si nanobeam (~200 nm long) sits between electrodes tied to the bitline pair; the differential tips it into one well, where it mechanically latches and touches a restore electrode, giving zero leakage and zero standby power.
why: Periphery (#7) and idle power: zero SA leakage in a ~0.05 um^2 footprint from silicon alone; 10-50 ns switching restricts it to capacity tiers.

title: Resonant LC tank charges wordlines adiabatically and recycles energy
idea: Worse: slam 3 V wordlines up from ground and dump their charge to ground on every activation. Flip: drive the selected wordline group from a package-level inductor in a resonant loop that ramps it up sinusoidally and swings the charge back into the tank, or into the next wordline, on deactivation.
why: Voltage floor and activation energy (fact 10): recovers ~50-70% of wordline CV^2 energy and offloads the VPP pumps.

title: Half-size canary capacitors trigger subarray refresh on demand
idea: MINIFY a few sentinel cells on purpose: each 512-row subarray carries 8 canary cells with half-size capacitors and deliberately leaky access devices; a low-power comparator polls them and refreshes the subarray only when a canary decays below threshold.
why: Fact 3: refresh tracks actual retention instead of the 13 fA worst-case tail, cutting refresh operations 4-10x at typical temperatures.

title: Canary in coal mine: leaky sentinel cells set refresh pace
idea: Place 8 canary cells per mat whose access transistors are drawn ~15% shorter so they leak ~3x faster than the worst real cell; during idle the SA checks them every few ms and the mat is refreshed only after a canary flips, so the refresh period tracks real temperature and process instead of a fixed 32-64 ms worst case.
why: Refresh tax (fact 3: 16-33% of idle power, 10-20% of bandwidth): typical dies and temperatures retain far longer than spec, so mat-level adaptive refresh can stretch intervals 2-4x safely.

title: Canary rows for row hammer: deliberately weak sentinel cells
idea: Miners carried canaries because they faint first. Every 32 rows include a sentinel row with smaller capacitors holding a known pattern; the SA stripe checks the sentinels when their neighbors activate, and a sentinel flip triggers targeted refresh nearby before real data can flip.
why: Senses real disturbance instead of counting activations, adapting to each die's actual ~1k hammer threshold (fact 9) at ~3% area, transparent to the bus.

title: Frequency-division wordline decoding with resonant driver gates
idea: Limit: zero logic gates in the row decoder. Each wordline-driver group is gated by a tiny resonant element (BAW or varactor tank) tuned to a unique frequency pair; the bank broadcasts two tones on one shared line, and only the group resonant at both rectifies enough voltage to fire, so address-to-frequency replaces the NAND decode tree.
why: Removes multi-stage decoder trees and predecode buses (~8-10% of the die) and frees one routing metal. Feasibility hinges on resonator size versus pitch, so it applies at subarray-select granularity, not per wordline.

title: Synaptic-vesicle charge packets shifted by bucket brigade to edge amplifiers
idea: Instead of a sense amp on every bitline pair, the activated row's charges move as discrete packets (like vesicles to a release site) through CCD-style transfer gates under each bitline. They reach a few high-quality correlated amplifiers at the mat edge, which digitize and write back by reverse transfer.
why: Fact 7: one amplifier per ~32 bitlines cuts sense-amp stripe area ~70% (~12-15% of the die). Random latency gets worse, so it suits streaming/AI-weight memory tiers.

title: Pulse-width-weighted reads: one integrator resolves four NV bits
idea: Constraint: non-volatile cells with ON/OFF ratio above 50x (ReRAM/FTJ). Four cells on one bitline are read at once with wordline pulse widths of 1:2:4:8, so their currents integrate on one capacitor as a binary-weighted charge, and a 4-bit SAR converter returns all four bits.
why: Periphery (fact 7): sense-amp count and read energy per bit fall ~4x; the read is non-destructive so it needs no restore.

title: Snapback counting reads N stacked threshold cells per crosspoint
idea: Failure mined: Optane died partly because each extra deck needed its own lithography and decoders, so cost never scaled past two decks. Fix: deposit 8 chalcogenide threshold-switching memory layers in series at every crosspoint, pattern them with one etch, and engineer a different threshold window for each layer. One voltage ramp per pillar is read by counting and timing the snapback current spikes, whose pattern encodes all 8 states.
why: 10x at the same cost: 8 bits per 4F^2 crosspoint vs 1 bit per 6F^2 is ~12x density, with one patterning step and one decoder set shared by all 8 layers, so decks no longer multiply masks.

title: Same-age reference cells let the sense threshold follow leakage decay
idea: Failure mined: resistance drift ate Optane's PCM read window until drift-tracking reads were added. Fix for DRAM: every row carries 4 reference cells written with 1s and 0s in the same activation as the data. At read they are charge-shared onto the reference bitline, so the threshold falls in step as stored 1s leak instead of sitting fixed at VBL/2.
why: Refresh (fact 3): a decaying 1 stays above an equally decaying midpoint for longer, roughly 2-3x the usable retention. That cuts refresh energy and bandwidth loss 50-65% for ~0.5% array overhead.

title: Superconducting nanowire-loop memory with single-flux-quantum sensing
idea: Inverting 'memory sensing is analog voltage at room temperature': bits are clockwise or counter-clockwise persistent currents in kinetic-inductance nanowire loops at 4 K, read by a single-flux-quantum comparator that switches only for one current direction, for cryogenic AI and quantum-control racks.
why: Read energy ~1e-18 J with no leakage and no refresh; periphery in SFQ logic. Density and cooling cost make it speculative.

title: 4 K cryo-DRAM with single-electron-transistor sensing for qubit controllers
idea: Quantum computers need working memory inside the cryostat: at 4 K leakage is zero and single-electron transistors are practical electrometers, so cells store ~20-50 electrons and an SET coupled to each storage node reads them. Lessons on charge-limit sensing feed room-temperature small-island designs.
why: Refresh-free with ~100x less charge per bit and opens a new cryo-memory niche; generalizing to 300 K is speculative.

title: Mars electrodynamic dust shield built into the wafer chuck
idea: Mars and lunar solar panels shed dust with a traveling-wave field from embedded electrodes. Build interleaved 3-phase electrodes into the electrostatic chucks and load locks of periphery dry tools, hopping charged particles off the wafer into a vacuum trap between steps instead of sending wafers to scrubber rinses.
why: Water: post-step brush/spray scrubs in periphery modules (~5-10 L each) fall ~10x, and particles are caught before they become defects.

title: Abacus beads: successive-approximation sensing reads two bits per cell
idea: Read like sliding abacus beads one rank at a time: after charge sharing a 2-step SAR sense amp compares against a mid reference for the MSB, then switches in a binary-weighted half-step reference capacitor to resolve the LSB, and a 4-level write driver restores one of four voltages.
why: Density and cost per bit ~2x with the same capacitor, but it needs ~3-4x signal, so it must pair with a gain or low-C_BL idea; adds ~20% SA area.

title: Chain DRAM: Toshiba's chain-FeRAM topology with linear capacitors
idea: Failure mined: Toshiba's chain FeRAM (each capacitor in parallel with its transistor, 16 in series) died with Toshiba's FeRAM exit and its plate-pulse complexity. Fix: build the chain with ordinary DRAM linear capacitors. To read cell k, turn off only its transistor so its capacitor sits in series between the chain and the bitline; one bitline contact serves 16 cells and no plate pulsing is needed.
why: 16x fewer bitline contacts cut bitline capacitance ~40%, which raises the signal. Bitlines can then be 1.5-2x longer with proportionally fewer sense amps, and the cell gets denser without contacts.

title: Continuity: rolling-scan drum memory needs only a shift-register row scanner
idea: TRIZ #20 Continuity of useful action: like a display gate driver, a shift register sweeps every row in order, sensing and restoring each (so refresh is the scan itself) and presenting each row to a page buffer as it passes; requests wait for their row to come around, removing row address decoders, refresh logic and most control.
why: 100x path: row periphery shrinks to a TFT gate-driver-on-array strip (~1-2% of area) buildable on glass or BEOL lines and repeatable in stacked tiers; trade-offs: average latency is half a scan (~5-30 us), so it suits streaming and batched AI tensors. Attacks Facts 3 and 7.

title: Frequency-multiplexed wordline group select borrowed from MKID astronomy arrays
idea: MKID cameras read thousands of detectors on one feedline by giving each a unique resonance; each wordline group taps a shared global line through a passive high-Q LC notch tuned to its own frequency, and a tone burst on the line selects that group. Global predecoder wiring collapses to one line per bank.
why: Row-decoder and global wiring area (part of fact 7's 49%) cut sharply; speculative because on-die high-Q resonators are large and slow to ring up.

title: S: sulfide threshold-switch matrix replaces per-wordline decoder transistors
idea: Place a two-terminal sulfide-based Ovonic threshold switch between each local wordline and two crossing global select lines; only the wordline at the driven intersection sees enough voltage to snap its switch on, so N wordlines need only ~2 sqrt(N) drivers.
why: Turns O(N) decoder/driver transistors into O(sqrt N) with BEOL two-terminal devices, roughly halving row-periphery area (fact 7); risks are half-select leakage and switch endurance at ~1e15 cycles.

title: Self-decoding array builds decoders from vertical array transistors
idea: Instead of separate periphery CMOS, implement the row predecoder as a NAND-style ROM matrix made of the same vertical-channel transistors as the array, pitch-matched at array density and fabricated in the same steps.
why: Periphery area and process cost (facts 4, 7): decoder area ~3-5x smaller, fewer periphery masks.

title: Weak canary bitlines trigger refresh only when decay is real
idea: Box: pillar cap x Si access x dedicated canary comparator x per-mat monitor x bulk Si x standard flow. Each mat carries a column of deliberately leaky cells (narrowed access gate) whose decay a reference comparator watches; that mat is refreshed only when the canaries cross threshold, tracking temperature and process automatically.
why: Refresh (~46 fJ/bit, 16-33% of idle power) cut 3-5x at typical temperatures; bandwidth loss down.

title: Decay-as-weight-decay memory for training master weights
idea: Time-shift the meaning of leakage: master weights and optimizer moments are rewritten every training step (~1 s), so they sit in refresh-free DRAM where MSBs use double-size robust cells and low mantissa bits use tiny cells whose 1->0 decay acts as stochastic rounding toward zero, a built-in weight decay.
why: Zero refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3) and ~30% more bits per area for low-order bits (fact 1).
